newsitem.title: INDIA: Status report on India's external debt.
newsitem.headline: Status report on India's external debt.

text.p: Following is the text of a statement on India's external debt issued by the Finance Ministry on Thursday:
The external debt position of India has improved steadily in the recent years.
The absolute level of debt declined for the first time in the recent past from the peak of $99.01 billion at the end of March 1995 to $92.20 billion at the end of March 1996.

The debt-service ratio which reached a high of 35.3 percent in 1990/91 has come down more or less steadily to 25.5 percent in 1995/96. Similarly, the debt-GDP ratio declined from the peak of 41 percent in 1991/92 to 28.7 percent in 1995/96. The table below gives certain key external debt ratios since 1990/91.
Year Debt Service Interest/Current Debt/GDP Debt/Current
Source:Government of India, Ministry of Finance.
About 75 percent of the decline in debt stock between end-March 1995 and end-March 1996 could be attributed to the appreciation of the U.S. dollar against major international currencies.

However, as much as $1.69 billion out of the total decline of $6.81 billion is real - the decline would have taken place even if the cross rates between U.S dollar and other currencies had remained unchanged.

A salient feature of India's external debt is the high share of concessional debt. This has remained steady at around 45 percent in recent years. The ratio of short-term debt to total debt, which reached 10.20 percent at the end of March 1991, came down steadily to 3.9 percent at the end of March 1994. The ratio stood at 5.5 percent at the end of 1996. India is favourably placed vis-a-vis other major developing country debtors regarding concessional and short term components of debt.

The share of debt from bilateral and multilateral sources (including International Monetary Fund and rupee debt) has remained steady at around two-thirds of the total long-term debt since 1990. Private creditors including commercial sources, export credit agencies and non-resident Indians have accounted for the balance one-third.

The fact that these shares have remained unchanged suggests that there is no truth in the belief that the shares of debt from private sources has considerably increased over time and those from multilateral and bilateral sources have declined.

While the improvements on the external debt front are a welcome sign, the emphasis now has to be on consolidating the existing gains and bringing debt to more manageable levels through sustaining the momentum of export growth, effective management of the existing debt and careful planning of future borrowings.
